title: SpecKCast: Spectral Kalman Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration

paper.title: SpecKCast: Spectral Kalman Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity image and video generation, but they suffer from substantial inference costs due to repeated transformer evaluations across many denoising steps. Feature caching reduces this cost by reusing features across denoising steps. Recent forecasting methods extend this idea by extrapolating features to skipped steps instead of reusing them. However, existing forecasting methods extrapolate the features they predict uniformly, even though the spatial-frequency components of these features change most at different stages of denoising. They also overlook that denoising progresses nonuniformly, so equal step intervals can correspond to very different amounts of change. These mismatches amplify forecast errors as more steps are skipped, limiting the achievable acceleration. We propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that forecasts the model output in the frequency domain. SpecKCast applies a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the output and tracks each coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter along a band-specific time coordinate derived from the noise schedule. The filter tracks each coefficient’s value and rate of change, and the transformer is evaluated only when the filter’s forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo show that SpecKCast achieves a better trade-off between acceleration and fidelity than existing caching and forecasting methods, reaching up to 6 × 6\times speedup with less than 0.05 GiB of additional memory.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity visual generation, gaining significant attention from recent advances in image and video generation. Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) further improved generation quality by enabling greater model capacity. However, their costly forward passes throughout many denoising steps lead to substantially higher inference latency, limiting their use in real-time applications. To address this bottleneck, a wide range of acceleration techniques have been proposed to reduce either the step count or the per-step cost, including efficient attention ( Xia et al., 2025 ) , step distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , and quantization ( Li et al., 2023 ) . Among these, feature caching has emerged as a practical, training-free approach. Motivated by the observation that model outputs are highly similar across adjacent timesteps, these methods cache features from previous steps and reuse them in subsequent ones, skipping substantial computation ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) . However, this similarity decays as the gap between timesteps grows, so naive reuse over longer spans significantly degrades generation quality, limiting caching to modest acceleration ratios. To address this, recent work shifts from reusing features to forecasting them ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Rather than assuming that a cached feature remains valid at a later timestep, forecasting methods exploit temporal continuity along the denoising trajectory, using features from previous steps to estimate their evolution and extrapolate their values at the target timestep. By modeling temporal drift, forecasting remains effective across wider timestep gaps, enabling higher acceleration ratios at comparable generation quality. Despite their promise, existing forecasting approaches impose uniformity on both what they forecast and how they model the signal over time ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . First, they extrapolate the model output or feature representation as a whole, or apply the same forecasting rule uniformly to all of its components (e.g., channels), even though the spatial-frequency components of the signal evolve very differently. As Figure 2 shows, low-frequency content changes sharply in the first few steps and then settles, while high-frequency content changes slightly at first but evolves rapidly toward the end. Because these bands are active at different stages, a single uniform forecaster may not serve them all. Second, existing methods use the sampler’s step index or raw diffusion timestep as their temporal coordinate, even though the amount of denoising performed at each step is nonuniform and depends on the scheduler. Therefore, equal intervals in the chosen coordinate can represent very different amounts of denoising progress. Treating these intervals as equivalent makes the resulting trajectory harder to model and forecast. Together, these limitations restrict achievable acceleration, amplify forecast errors, and degrade generation quality as the skip length increases. Motivated by this insight, we propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that rethinks both what we forecast and how we extrapolate. The key idea is to forecast the model’s temporal evolution separately in the frequency domain, rather than uniformly in feature or latent space. SpecKCast transforms the model output into the spatial-frequency domain with a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT), and forecasts each coefficient during denoising. Moreover, instead of indexing the trajectory by the sampler’s timestep, SpecKCast exploits a time coordinate derived from the noise scheduler and applies a nonlinear time warping that improves the accuracy of local extrapolation within each band. To track each coefficient as it moves along its trajectory, SpecKCast uses a lightweight Kalman filter, a recursive state-space estimator that maintains the coefficient’s value and rate of change, projecting this state across a skip and correcting it after a full denoising step. The filter also estimates the uncertainty of each forecast. As more steps are skipped, this uncertainty increases, while the rate of change decays to keep the prediction stable. Furthermore, SpecKCast partitions the coefficients into frequency bands that share a common temporal coordinate and forecast uncertainty, while each coefficient keeps its own value and rate of change. Finally, at skipped steps, the predicted coefficients are transformed back to the spatial domain and passed directly to the sampler. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. • Frequency-Decoupled and Scheduler-Aligned Forecasting. We introduce SpecKCast, a training-free method that decomposes the model output in the spatial-frequency domain and forecasts its components along a nonlinear time coordinate derived from the noise scheduler. • Uncertainty-Aware Kalman Forecasting. SpecKCast uses a lightweight Kalman filter to track frequency coefficient trajectories and leverage forecast uncertainty to maintain stability over skipped denoising steps. • State-of-the-Art Performance. SpecKCast consistently improves the acceleration and generation quality trade-off over existing caching and forecasting methods while introducing negligible computational and memory overhead, requiring about 5 MiB of additional memory for FLUX.1 ( Labs, 2024 ) . sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) have become a leading approach for image and video generation. Since the introduction of the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , many works have built on this architecture, achieving strong results across diverse domains ( Chen et al., 2024a ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Rajabi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . This progress, however, comes at a cost. Sampling requires many sequential forward passes through a large network, making inference slow and expensive. This limits practical applications and has made diffusion model acceleration an important research direction. A large body of work has therefore focused on reducing sampling steps, mostly by distilling a multi-step teacher into a few-step student ( Meng et al., 2023 ) . Examples include consistency models ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ) and DMD ( Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ) . Although effective, these approaches require additional training and are prone to reduced sample diversity. A more recent line of work explores feature caching, which accelerates inference without any additional training. The core idea is to reuse intermediate features across timesteps to avoid redundant computation ( Zou et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) . Early methods such as DeepCache ( Ma et al., 2024 ) accelerated the U-Net backbone using handcrafted caching rules, and Δ \Delta -DiT ( Chen et al., 2024b ) later extended this idea to DiT architectures. Subsequent methods further refine what and when to cache. FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) reuses attention and MLP outputs across timesteps, while TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) exploits the correlation between timestep embeddings and model outputs to estimate how much the output changes between steps and decide when to reuse cached features. HiCache ( Feng et al., 2026 ) forecasts features with scaled Hermite polynomials to capture their non-monotonic dynamics in DiTs. SeaCache ( Chung et al., 2026 ) instead improves the caching decision by measuring feature changes after a spectral filter that preserves content-relevant components and suppresses noise. However, feature similarity decreases as the timestep gap increases. As more steps are skipped, the cached features deviate further from the actual ones, and these errors accumulate during sampling. This causes the trajectory to drift and degrades generation quality, limiting the achievable speedup. To address this, recent work shifts from reusing features to forecasting them ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Instead of assuming that cached features remain valid at later timesteps, forecasting methods use features from previous steps to predict how they evolve and estimate their values at the target timestep. TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025b ) does this locally with a Taylor expansion, using finite differences of the most recent cached features, while Spectrum ( Han et al., 2026 ) fits a Chebyshev expansion over the full feature history to better capture long-range dynamics. By modeling how features evolve, these methods remain effective over wider timestep gaps, enabling higher acceleration at comparable quality. However, both forecast uniformly in feature space and along the sampler’s timestep, ignoring that denoising progress is nonuniform across steps. In contrast, SpecKCast forecasts each frequency band separately along a scheduler-derived time axis, using a lightweight Kalman filter that adapts its forecasts as the trajectory evolves.

sections.heading: 3.1 Diffusion Models and Flow Matching
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) define a generative process that gradually transforms samples from a simple prior (e.g., Gaussian) into data via a learned reverse-time process. Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) instead learns a velocity field that transports noise to data along near-straight paths. Both are instances of stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) , with x t = α t ​ x 0 + σ t ​ ϵ x_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon , where rectified flow sets α t = 1 − t \alpha_{t}=1-t and σ t = t \sigma_{t}=t and learns the velocity v = ϵ − x 0 v=\epsilon-x_{0} . Sampling integrates the reverse flow over decreasing noise levels using Euler updates: x j + 1 = x j + ( σ j + 1 − σ j ) ​ Y j , Y j = v θ ​ ( x j , σ j , c ) , x_{j+1}=x_{j}+(\sigma_{j+1}-\sigma_{j})Y_{j},\qquad Y_{j}=v_{\theta}(x_{j},\sigma_{j},c), (1) where c c denotes the text condition. We measure denoising cost by the number of function evaluations (NFE), defined as the number of denoising steps at which the transformer is evaluated; for models with classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , each such step includes both passes.

sections.heading: 3.2 Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration
sections.text: Adjacent denoising steps produce highly correlated features and outputs, allowing redundant computation to be avoided ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Forecasting exploits this temporal redundancy by predicting skipped signals from past observations. Let 𝒰 ⊆ { 0 , … , N − 1 } \mathcal{U}\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N-1\} denote the steps that evaluate the denoiser. For output-level forecasting, Y ^ j = f ⁡ ( h j , j ) , j ∉ 𝒰 , \widehat{Y}_{j}=f(h_{j},j),\qquad j\notin\mathcal{U}, (2) where h j h_{j} encodes past outputs and Y ^ j \widehat{Y}_{j} replaces Y j Y_{j} in the sampler. Forecasting may instead target intermediate features, making the choice of forecast target and representation a key design decision.

sections.text: The Kalman filter ( Kalman, 1960 ) is a classical method that recursively estimates the state of a dynamic signal from intermittent observations. An important property of the Kalman filter is that it is fully online, requiring a constant number of operations and no window of past observations to store or refit, so a large number of signals can be tracked in parallel at negligible cost. Between observations, the filter advances the state, while the covariance grows to reflect increasing forecast uncertainty, making the filter suitable for forecasting over extended gaps between observations.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: Spec tral K alman Fore Cast ing (SpecKCast) is an inference-time acceleration method for DiTs that reduces transformer evaluations during denoising. Unlike feature-caching methods that approximate an intermediate activation and still execute the remaining network layers, SpecKCast models the final velocity consumed by the sampler. SpecKCast applies a 2D DCT to the model output and forecasts each frequency coefficient individually, while partitioning coefficients into bands that share forecast uncertainty and a noise-schedule-derived time coordinate, warped nonlinearly to better align with each band’s temporal evolution. SpecKCast uses a Kalman filter to track each DCT coefficient’s value and temporal derivative, while sharing covariance statistics within each frequency band. The predicted coefficients are transformed back to the spatial domain and passed directly to the sampler.

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Spatial-frequency Decomposition
sections.text: Forecasting the entire transformer output with a single temporal model ignores an important property of diffusion predictions: different spatial frequencies exhibit different temporal dynamics, as shown in Figure 2 . Low-frequency content settles early and drifts slowly, while high-frequency content remains active until the end of sampling. To account for these distinct dynamics, SpecKCast transforms each output into the spatial-frequency domain and forecasts its coefficients separately. Given the denoiser output Y j ∈ ℝ C × H × W Y_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} at timestep j j , we apply an orthonormal 2D DCT independently to each channel, Z j = DCT 2 ​ D ⁡ ( Y j ) Z_{j}=\operatorname{DCT}_{2\mathrm{D}}(Y_{j}) , and partition the frequency plane into L L non-overlapping radial bands. Each frequency coefficient is treated as a separate temporal signal and forecast by its own predictor, while the band determines how each coefficient’s dynamics are modeled. On steps where the transformer computes the full denoising step, the observed Z j Z_{j} updates the predictors; on skipped steps, the forecasters extrapolate each coefficient’s trajectory and together form Z ^ j \widehat{Z}_{j} . The forecast is then transformed back to the spatial domain, Y ^ j = IDCT 2 ​ D ⁡ ( Z ^ j ) \widehat{Y}_{j}=\operatorname{IDCT}_{2\mathrm{D}}(\widehat{Z}_{j}) , and passed directly to the diffusion sampler.

sections.text: Each coefficient in SpecKCast is forecast as a function of time, which raises the question of what to use as the time variable. A natural choice is the step index j j , but it does not capture the nonuniform progression of the denoising process. As a result, equal increments of j j can correspond to very different amounts of change, making the trajectory harder to forecast. We instead derive the time variable from the noise schedule , expressed as the log signal-to-noise ratio λ j = 2 ​ log ⁡ ( ( 1 − σ j ) / σ j ) \lambda_{j}=2\log\!\big((1-\sigma_{j})/\sigma_{j}\big) . A band’s trajectory therefore bends where the band is most active and stays flat where it is not, making it nonlinear in λ j \lambda_{j} . What the forecaster needs is a time variable whose increments reflect how much each band is expected to evolve. sections.heading: 4.3 Uncertainty-Aware Scheduling
sections.text: The remaining question is which steps to compute. A fixed schedule is the simplest choice, but it cannot respond to changes in forecasting difficulty across generations and denoising phases. This requires combining the per-band covariances into a single decision quantity. Coefficients within the same band share the covariance P ℓ , j P_{\ell,j} because they use the same time coordinate and process-noise model. sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: For text-to-image generation, we use the DrawBench ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) prompts and report ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) and CLIP Score ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) , which measures text–image alignment. For text-to-video generation, we follow the standard prompts and protocol of VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and report its Quality Score, which aggregates dimensions such as temporal consistency, motion smoothness, and per-frame aesthetic and imaging quality. Since an accelerated sampler should reproduce the output of the full model rather than merely produce a plausible sample, we also compare each accelerated sample with its 50-step reference generated from the same prompt and seed. We report PSNR for pixel-level error, SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) for structural similarity, and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for perceptual distance. For efficiency, we report sampling latency, speedup over the 50-step reference, and memory overhead (Mem. Δ \Delta ), defined as the peak allocated GPU memory above that of Base at the same NFE. sections.heading: 5.1 Text-to-image Generation
sections.text: Table 1 reports results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image, where Base runs the original sampler with fewer steps to match the NFE. SpecKCast achieves the highest speedup among acceleration methods in all but one setting, along with the best PSNR and LPIPS in all settings and the best SSIM in all but one. At the highest acceleration, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 1.1 dB PSNR on FLUX.1-dev ( 5.54 × 5.54\times ) and 2.0 dB on Qwen-Image ( 6.00 × 6.00\times ). Spectrum, the closest competitor at 14 and 10 NFE, trails SpecKCast by 0.5–1.4 dB PSNR and degrades sharply on Qwen-Image at 8 NFE, where its LPIPS rises to 0.527 compared with 0.267 for SpecKCast. Compared with Base, which runs at a similar speed, SpecKCast improves PSNR by 5.5–9.0 dB, showing that it tracks the 50-step trajectory far more closely than simply taking fewer steps. These gains cost at most 0.01 GiB of memory, whereas TaylorSeer, HiCache, and Spectrum add 0.73–18.97 GiB. Figures 3 and 6 show qualitative results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image, respectively. TaylorSeer and HiCache blur the images, TeaCache and SeaCache alter textures and lighting, and every baseline misspells or distorts the text on the sign. SpecKCast stays closest to the 50-step reference while running fastest. More samples are provided in Appendix F .

sections.heading: 5.2 Text-to-video Generation
sections.text: Table 2 reports results on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo. SpecKCast achieves the highest or near-highest speedup in every setting, along with the best SSIM in all settings and the best PSNR and LPIPS in most. On HunyuanVideo at the 14-NFE budget, it improves PSNR by 2.1 dB over SeaCache, the strongest baseline, while running at 3.33 × 3.33\times instead of 2.57 × 2.57\times . The advantage holds at the 8-NFE budget, where SpecKCast keeps the best SSIM and LPIPS on both models, while HiCache and TaylorSeer drop to 12.06 and 13.02 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-14B. SpecKCast also achieves the best VBench Quality on Wan2.1-14B at every budget, staying within 0.25 points of the reference at the 14-NFE budget. Spectrum obtains slightly lower LPIPS on Wan2.1-14B at the 14- and 10-NFE budgets, but requires up to 13.12 GiB of extra memory, compared with 0.05 GiB for SpecKCast. Figures 4 and 6 show qualitative results on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1-14B, respectively. On HunyuanVideo, most baselines replace the puffin in the first frame with a blurred or different bird, and SeaCache adds a second cat in later frames. On Wan2.1-14B, the baselines introduce local artifacts (red boxes), mostly in the window background, and HiCache also shifts the lighting. SpecKCast stays closest to the 50-step reference across frames on both models.

sections.heading: 5.3 Ablation Studies
sections.text: Table 3 ablates the components of SpecKCast on FLUX.1-dev at 14 NFE. Since uncertainty-aware scheduling relies on the Kalman covariance, we first compare forecasters under a fixed schedule. Kalman and Taylor perform similarly, with Kalman slightly faster and higher in PSNR, while Chebyshev is both slower and less accurate. With our frequency decomposition and time warping, the Taylor forecaster also outperforms TaylorSeer ( Table 1 ) by 4.2 dB PSNR while reducing latency from 4.59 to 3.46 s. Replacing the fixed schedule with uncertainty-aware scheduling ( Section 4.3 ) improves PSNR by 2.2 dB. Band-specific time warping ( Section 4.1.2 ) outperforms the raw log-SNR λ j \lambda_{j} by 3.3 dB and the step index j j by 4.7 dB, and removing the frequency decomposition lowers PSNR by 3.1 dB. Overall, the full model achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and ImageReward. Since all variants except Chebyshev run within 0.1 s of each other, these gains come at almost no extra latency.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented SpecKCast, a training-free method for accelerating Diffusion Transformers by forecasting the denoiser output at skipped sampling steps. Rather than modeling the output uniformly, SpecKCast decomposes it into spatial-frequency components and forecasts their distinct temporal dynamics along band-specific, noise-schedule-aligned time coordinates. A lightweight Kalman filter tracks the value and rate of change of each DCT coefficient, while its uncertainty provides a principled signal for adaptively determining when a full transformer evaluation is needed. Across image and video diffusion models, SpecKCast consistently improves the acceleration–quality trade-off over existing caching and forecasting methods, achieving the best fidelity to the 50-step reference in most settings with negligible latency and memory overhead. These results highlight the benefit of explicitly accounting for the distinct temporal evolution of frequency components when forecasting diffusion trajectories. SpecKCast, however, targets only temporal redundancy across denoising steps; each computed step still processes the full token grid and therefore retains the spatial redundancy within a transformer evaluation. Jointly exploiting temporal and spatial redundancy could enable further acceleration and represents a promising direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Kalman Filter
sections.text: The Kalman filter ( Kalman, 1960 ) is the exact Bayesian estimator for a linear-Gaussian state-space model. A hidden state h j h_{j} evolves linearly and is observed with noise, h j = A j ​ h j − 1 + w j , w j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Q j ) , y j = H j ​ h j + η j , η j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , R j ) . h_{j}=A_{j}h_{j-1}+w_{j},\quad w_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Q_{j}),\qquad y_{j}=H_{j}h_{j}+\eta_{j},\quad\eta_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R_{j}). (13) The filter represents its estimate of h j h_{j} as a Gaussian with mean h ^ j \hat{h}_{j} and covariance P j P_{j} , and alternates between two operations. Between observations, it predicts the next state, h ^ j ← A j ​ h ^ j − 1 \hat{h}_{j}\leftarrow A_{j}\hat{h}_{j-1} and P j ← A j ​ P j − 1 ​ A j ⊤ + Q j P_{j}\leftarrow A_{j}P_{j-1}A_{j}^{\top}+Q_{j} , so the estimate moves forward and its uncertainty grows. When an observation is available, it updates the prediction using the gain K j = P j ​ H j ⊤ ​ ( H j ​ P j ​ H j ⊤ + R j ) − 1 K_{j}=P_{j}H_{j}^{\top}(H_{j}P_{j}H_{j}^{\top}+R_{j})^{-1} , h ^ j ← h ^ j + K j ​ ( y j − H j ​ h ^ j ) ⏟ prediction residual , P j ← ( I − K j ​ H j ) ​ P j . \hat{h}_{j}\leftarrow\hat{h}_{j}+K_{j}\underbrace{(y_{j}-H_{j}\hat{h}_{j})}_{\text{prediction residual}},\qquad P_{j}\leftarrow(I-K_{j}H_{j})\,P_{j}. (14) The prediction residual is the part of the observation that the prediction did not account for. Under the model, its variance is H j ​ P j ​ H j ⊤ + R j H_{j}P_{j}H_{j}^{\top}+R_{j} . Comparing the observed residuals with this variance shows whether the assumed noise levels are too low or too high, which allows the filter to adjust them during inference. For a smooth signal whose rate of change is unknown and varies slowly, a common choice of state is the local linear trend , h = ( m , ν ) ⊤ h=(m,\nu)^{\top} , where m m is the value and ν \nu is its rate of change. The value integrates the rate, and the rate is perturbed by white noise. Both the transition and the process noise then depend only on the time Δ \Delta elapsed between steps, A ⁡ ( Δ ) = ( 1 Δ 0 1 ) , Q ⁡ ( Δ ) = q ​ ( Δ 3 / 3 Δ 2 / 2 Δ 2 / 2 Δ ) , A(\Delta)=\begin{pmatrix}1&\Delta\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q(\Delta)=q\begin{pmatrix}\Delta^{3}/3&\Delta^{2}/2\\[2.0pt] \Delta^{2}/2&\Delta\end{pmatrix}, (15) where Q ⁡ ( Δ ) Q(\Delta) is the covariance accumulated when the rate is perturbed by white noise of intensity q q . SpecKCast uses this model with an additional damping factor on the rate ( Section 4 ). This model has three properties that make it suitable for the forecasting problem in Eq. 2 . First, the predicted value is the minimum-mean-squared-error estimate under the model and depends on all past observations. When the rate is poorly determined, the gain reduces its influence on the forecast. A finite-difference forecaster instead relies only on the most recent observations and amplifies their noise. Second, the filter handles irregularly spaced observations directly, because Δ \Delta enters A A and Q Q . Fixed-order difference formulas assume uniform spacing, which an adaptive compute schedule does not provide. Third, the predicted covariance P P is available before the next observation, so the filter estimates its own forecast error. This lets us choose the compute steps 𝒰 \mathcal{U} by thresholding the predicted error rather than with a hand-designed schedule. The Kalman filter is related to the Wiener filter, which is the optimal linear filter for a stationary signal in stationary noise and is defined by a fixed frequency response. The Kalman filter is its recursive counterpart for non-stationary signals: it tracks an evolving state together with its uncertainty. The filter itself is standard. Our contribution is the state-space model we place on the denoiser output and the way its covariance is calibrated and used for scheduling ( Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Appendix B Details of the Band-specific Time Warp
sections.text: This appendix expands on the time variable introduced in Section 4.1.2 . We derive the interpretation of λ j + log ⁡ p ℓ \lambda_{j}+\log p_{\ell} as the band’s own signal-to-noise ratio, describe the mechanics of the warp, and collect the implementation details omitted from the main text.

sections.heading: B.1 The Warped Quantity is the Band’s Own Log-SNR
sections.text: Recall that a noisy latent is a linear interpolation between data and noise, x σ = ( 1 − σ ) ​ x 0 + σ ​ ϵ x_{\sigma}=(1-\sigma)\,x_{0}+\sigma\,\epsilon with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) . Because the DCT is orthonormal, transforming white Gaussian noise yields white Gaussian noise, so every frequency coefficient of the noise term has unit variance and the noise contributes power σ 2 \sigma^{2} uniformly to every band. The data term is not uniform. Latents of natural images concentrate energy at low frequencies, so the coefficients of band ℓ \ell carry an average signal power p ℓ p_{\ell} that decreases with frequency. The signal-to-noise ratio of band ℓ \ell at noise level σ j \sigma_{j} is therefore approximately SNR ℓ ​ ( σ j ) = ( 1 − σ j ) 2 ​ p ℓ σ j 2 ⟹ log ⁡ SNR ℓ ​ ( σ j ) = 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 − σ j σ j ) ⏟ λ j + log ⁡ p ℓ . \mathrm{SNR}_{\ell}(\sigma_{j})\;=\;\frac{(1-\sigma_{j})^{2}\,p_{\ell}}{\sigma_{j}^{2}}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\log\mathrm{SNR}_{\ell}(\sigma_{j})\;=\;\underbrace{2\log\!\big(\tfrac{1-\sigma_{j}}{\sigma_{j}}\big)}_{\lambda_{j}}\;+\;\log p_{\ell}. (16) The sigmoid in Eq. 8 is therefore applied to the band’s own log-SNR, scaled by 1 / T w 1/T_{w} . Its argument crosses zero when SNR ℓ = 1 \mathrm{SNR}_{\ell}=1 , the point at which the band’s signal emerges from the noise. Since p ℓ p_{\ell} is large for low bands and small for high bands, low bands cross this threshold early in denoising (at large σ j \sigma_{j} ) and high bands cross it late, which explains why different bands do most of their changing in different phases.

sections.heading: B.2 Mechanics of the Warp
sections.text: The sigmoid maps the band’s scaled log-SNR to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) , and its derivative is largest at the zero crossing and decays symmetrically away from it. Consequently, most of the increase in the warped time t ℓ ​ ( j ) = sigmoid ⁡ ( ( λ j + log ⁡ p ℓ ) / T w ) t_{\ell}(j)=\operatorname{sigmoid}\big((\lambda_{j}+\log p_{\ell})/T_{w}\big) occurs during the steps around the band’s emergence, and t ℓ t_{\ell} barely moves while the band is still dominated by noise or has already settled. The temperature T w T_{w} sets the width of this active window in log-SNR units; a small T w T_{w} concentrates the time variable tightly around the crossing, while a large T w T_{w} approaches a plain rescaling of λ j \lambda_{j} . We use T w = 2 T_{w}=2 for all bands and all models. Since σ j \sigma_{j} decreases monotonically over sampling, λ j \lambda_{j} increases monotonically, and both the sigmoid and the final rescaling are monotone maps. Each s ℓ s_{\ell} is therefore a strictly increasing function of the step index, a requirement for a valid time variable. The operator rescale [ − 1 , 1 ] \operatorname{rescale}_{[-1,1]} is the affine map taking the smallest and largest values of t ℓ t_{\ell} over the N N steps of the run to − 1 -1 and 1 1 , respectively. Since t ℓ t_{\ell} is increasing, these are its first and last values, so s ℓ ​ ( j ) = 2 ​ t ℓ ​ ( j ) − t ℓ ​ ( 0 ) t ℓ ​ ( N − 1 ) − t ℓ ​ ( 0 ) − 1 . s_{\ell}(j)=2\,\frac{t_{\ell}(j)-t_{\ell}(0)}{t_{\ell}(N-1)-t_{\ell}(0)}-1. (17) Every band’s time variable therefore spans the same interval regardless of where its active window lies. The warp interacts with the forecaster through the increments Δ ℓ , j = s ℓ ​ ( j ) − s ℓ ​ ( j − 1 ) \Delta_{\ell,j}=s_{\ell}(j)-s_{\ell}(j-1) , which serve as the effective step sizes of the per-band Kalman filters. During a band’s active window the increments are large, so the filter expects more change per step, injects more process noise, and damps its trend estimate faster; outside the window the increments are small and the filter treats the band as nearly static. The warp thus lets a single, simple dynamics model adapt its behavior to each band and phase without any per-step logic.

sections.heading: B.3 Implementation Details
sections.text: The following details matter for reproducing the coordinate exactly. First, rectified-flow pipelines typically apply a shift to the noise schedule, which for some models depends on the resolution, so the realized σ j \sigma_{j} differ from the nominal linearly spaced values. SpecKCast rebuilds the exact schedule the pipeline will use before sampling begins and computes all s ℓ ​ ( j ) s_{\ell}(j) from it, so the forecaster’s time coordinates line up with the transformer calls at any resolution and step count. Second, the endpoints of the schedule are clamped away from σ = 0 \sigma=0 and σ = 1 \sigma=1 before evaluating λ j \lambda_{j} to avoid infinities. The clamping changes only the first and last values of λ j \lambda_{j} , where the sigmoid is nearly flat, so its effect on s ℓ s_{\ell} is small. Third, the band powers p ℓ p_{\ell} are measured once during calibration ( Section B.4 ) from the implied clean latent x ^ 0 = x j − σ j ​ Y j \hat{x}_{0}=x_{j}-\sigma_{j}Y_{j} over the final steps of the calibration trajectories. Since the warp is a fixed elementwise function of the schedule, the entire coordinate system costs a few scalar operations per run and is computed once before sampling.

sections.heading: B.4 Band-Power Calibration
sections.text: SpecKCast uses p ℓ p_{\ell} to account for differences in signal magnitude across frequency bands. We estimate these values once per model from a small calibration set 𝒞 \mathcal{C} by running the unaccelerated model and recording the latent x j x_{j} , model output Y j Y_{j} , and noise level σ j \sigma_{j} at every denoising step. Under the rectified-flow interpolation, x j = ( 1 − σ j ) ​ x 0 + σ j ​ ϵ = x 0 + σ j ​ ( ϵ − x 0 ) . x_{j}=(1-\sigma_{j})x_{0}+\sigma_{j}\epsilon=x_{0}+\sigma_{j}(\epsilon-x_{0}). (18) Because the model predicts the velocity Y j ≈ ϵ − x 0 Y_{j}\approx\epsilon-x_{0} , it provides the clean-sample estimate x ^ 0 , j = x j − σ j ​ Y j . \widehat{x}_{0,j}=x_{j}-\sigma_{j}Y_{j}. (19) We estimate power using the later denoising steps, where σ j \sigma_{j} is smaller. In particular, if Y j = ( ϵ − x 0 ) + δ j , Y_{j}=(\epsilon-x_{0})+\delta_{j}, (20) then x ^ 0 , j = x 0 − σ j ​ δ j , \widehat{x}_{0,j}=x_{0}-\sigma_{j}\delta_{j}, (21) so velocity-prediction errors have less influence on x ^ 0 , j \widehat{x}_{0,j} near the end of denoising. We apply the same channel-wise orthonormal DCT used by SpecKCast, X 0 , j = DCT 2 ​ D ⁡ ( x ^ 0 , j ) . X_{0,j}=\operatorname{DCT}_{2\mathrm{D}}(\widehat{x}_{0,j}). (22) Let Ω ℓ \Omega_{\ell} contain the spatial-frequency indices belonging to band ℓ \ell . We estimate its signal power by averaging the squared DCT coefficients over calibration samples, selected denoising steps, channels, and frequencies: p ℓ = 1 | 𝒞 | ​ | 𝒥 | ​ C ​ | Ω ℓ | ​ ∑ n ∈ 𝒞 ∑ j ∈ 𝒥 ∑ c = 1 C ∑ ( u , v ) ∈ Ω ℓ | X 0 , j , c , u , v ( n ) | 2 , p_{\ell}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}||\mathcal{J}|C|\Omega_{\ell}|}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\sum_{(u,v)\in\Omega_{\ell}}\left|X_{0,j,c,u,v}^{(n)}\right|^{2}, (23) where 𝒥 \mathcal{J} denotes the selected denoising steps. Thus, p ℓ p_{\ell} shifts the global log-SNR according to the signal strength of each band, so the resulting coordinate reflects when that band transitions from noise-dominated to signal-dominated. In our implementation, the calibration uses 12 prompts with 50 denoising steps each, and 𝒥 \mathcal{J} contains the final 25 steps of each trajectory. The resulting p ℓ p_{\ell} are fixed across prompts during inference. Calibration modifies no model parameters and introduces no additional model evaluations at inference time.

sections.heading: Calibration-free alternatives.
sections.text: Offline calibration is not required to apply SpecKCast. The simplest alternative is to disable the band-specific warp and use rescaled log-SNR for every band, s ℓ ​ ( j ) = rescale [ − 1 , 1 ] ⁡ ( λ j ) . s_{\ell}(j)=\operatorname{rescale}_{[-1,1]}(\lambda_{j}). (24) Forecasting remains valid, but all bands then share the same temporal coordinate. Consequently, elapsed time no longer reflects their different signal-to-noise transitions, removing the band-specific control of extrapolation, damping, and uncertainty. This variant corresponds to the raw-logSNR row of Table 3 , where it lowers PSNR by 3.3 dB relative to the band-specific warp. When these outputs come from the warm-up steps ( Section D.2 ), this approach requires no additional transformer evaluations. However, the warm-up steps occur at the start of sampling, when the input is almost pure noise. The model output at these steps is therefore close to the noise itself, which has the same power in every band. As a result, the estimated p ℓ p_{\ell} is nearly the same for all bands and does not capture how signal power decreases with frequency. For this reason, all our experiments use the offline calibration described above.

sections.heading: B.5 Rationale for Band-Specific Time Reparameterization
sections.text: The denoising process follows one global sequence of steps j j and noise levels σ j \sigma_{j} . SpecKCast does not assign different physical denoising times to different frequency bands. Instead, it represents the same global step using a different increasing coordinate for each band: s ℓ ​ ( j ) = g ℓ ​ ( λ j ) , s_{\ell}(j)=g_{\ell}(\lambda_{j}), (26) where g ℓ g_{\ell} is the warp associated with band ℓ \ell . Because each g ℓ g_{\ell} is strictly increasing, the ordering of the denoising steps is preserved: j 1 < j 2 ⟹ s ℓ ​ ( j 1 ) < s ℓ ​ ( j 2 ) . j_{1}<j_{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s_{\ell}(j_{1})<s_{\ell}(j_{2}). (27) Thus, every band follows the same denoising direction and reaches the same target step, although the effective distance between two steps can differ across bands. For a skip from step j j to step k k , band ℓ \ell experiences the effective time interval Δ ℓ ​ ( j , k ) = s ℓ ​ ( k ) − s ℓ ​ ( j ) . \Delta_{\ell}(j,k)=s_{\ell}(k)-s_{\ell}(j). (28) This interval can be large for a band expected to change substantially during the skip and small for a band expected to remain stable. Consequently, the forecaster can make a larger update for an active band and a more conservative prediction for a stable one. This principle is not specific to the Kalman filter. Any forecasting model that uses time as an input, including linear extrapolation and polynomial fitting, can operate in a band-specific coordinate. The warp used by SpecKCast is g ℓ ​ ( λ ) = rescale [ − 1 , 1 ] ⁡ [ sigmoid ⁡ ( λ + log ⁡ p ℓ T w ) ] . g_{\ell}(\lambda)=\operatorname{rescale}_{[-1,1]}\left[\operatorname{sigmoid}\left(\frac{\lambda+\log p_{\ell}}{T_{w}}\right)\right]. (29) For p ℓ > 0 p_{\ell}>0 and T w > 0 T_{w}>0 , the sigmoid term is strictly increasing in λ \lambda , and the affine rescaling preserves this. The rescaling also gives all bands the same endpoints − 1 -1 and 1 1 , while their progression between these endpoints can differ.

sections.heading: Appendix C Details of the Kalman Forecaster
sections.text: The transition matrix A ℓ , j A_{\ell,j} and process-noise covariance Q ℓ , j Q_{\ell,j} serve different purposes. The former describes the expected evolution of a coefficient, while the latter represents deviations from that evolution. For coefficient i i in band ℓ \ell , the state is h i , j = ( m i , j , ν i , j ) , h_{i,j}=(m_{i,j},\nu_{i,j}), (30) where m i , j m_{i,j} is the coefficient value and ν i , j \nu_{i,j} is its temporal derivative. Over the interval Δ ℓ , j \Delta_{\ell,j} , we advance the value using its derivative and attenuate the derivative by ρ ℓ , j = exp ( − Δ ℓ , j / τ ℓ ) . \rho_{\ell,j}=\exp(-\Delta_{\ell,j}/\tau_{\ell}). (31) These operations give A ℓ , j = [ 1 Δ ℓ , j 0 ρ ℓ , j ] . A_{\ell,j}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\Delta_{\ell,j}\\ 0&\rho_{\ell,j}\end{bmatrix}. (32) The upper-right entry integrates the derivative over the interval, while the lower-right entry prevents old changes from being extrapolated indefinitely. As the interval grows, ρ ℓ , j \rho_{\ell,j} decreases and the prediction relies less on the previous derivative. The deterministic transition cannot capture all changes in the coefficient trajectory. We model these deviations as continuous random perturbations to the temporal derivative. If their intensity is q ℓ , j q_{\ell,j} and the damping is ignored, the accumulated state perturbation over an interval Δ ℓ , j \Delta_{\ell,j} has covariance Q ℓ , j = q ℓ , j ​ ∫ 0 Δ ℓ , j [ ( Δ ℓ , j − u ) 2 Δ ℓ , j − u Δ ℓ , j − u 1 ] ​ 𝑑 u , Q_{\ell,j}=q_{\ell,j}\int_{0}^{\Delta_{\ell,j}}\begin{bmatrix}(\Delta_{\ell,j}-u)^{2}&\Delta_{\ell,j}-u\\ \Delta_{\ell,j}-u&1\end{bmatrix}\,du, (33) which evaluates to Q ℓ , j = q ℓ , j ​ [ Δ ℓ , j 3 / 3 Δ ℓ , j 2 / 2 Δ ℓ , j 2 / 2 Δ ℓ , j ] . Q_{\ell,j}=q_{\ell,j}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta_{\ell,j}^{3}/3&\Delta_{\ell,j}^{2}/2\\ \Delta_{\ell,j}^{2}/2&\Delta_{\ell,j}\end{bmatrix}. (34) The lower-right term describes uncertainty accumulated in the temporal derivative. Integrating that uncertainty produces the cross-covariance terms and the cubic growth of uncertainty in the coefficient value. Consequently, longer forecast intervals result in larger covariance. The scalar q ℓ , j q_{\ell,j} controls the magnitude of this uncertainty. Bands with greater temporal activity receive larger process intensity, allowing their observations to produce stronger corrections. Since coefficients in the same band share Δ ℓ , j \Delta_{\ell,j} , ρ ℓ , j \rho_{\ell,j} , q ℓ , j q_{\ell,j} , and the observation noise, they also share A ℓ , j A_{\ell,j} , Q ℓ , j Q_{\ell,j} , and the resulting Kalman covariance, while retaining separate state estimates. This construction has intuitive limiting behavior. As Δ ℓ , j → 0 \Delta_{\ell,j}\rightarrow 0 , A ℓ , j → I A_{\ell,j}\rightarrow I and Q ℓ , j → 0 Q_{\ell,j}\rightarrow 0 , since little evolution or uncertainty is expected over a negligible interval. For longer intervals, the derivative is increasingly attenuated while process uncertainty grows. This transition is a stepwise discrete approximation rather than the exact discretization of a continuous damped system. It first advances the coefficient using the derivative at the beginning of each interval and then attenuates that derivative. Because the prediction is applied successively over all intervening denoising steps, the damping compounds across a multi-step skip.

sections.heading: D.2 Decision Rule
sections.text: After each computed step j j , the sidecar is rolled forward predictively , applying Equation 46 over a horizon of up to 10 10 future steps without changing its state, and the resulting risks R ⁡ ( j + 1 ) , R ⁡ ( j + 2 ) , … R(j{+}1),R(j{+}2),\dots are compared against the threshold. The next computed step is placed at the first predicted crossing R > ε R>\varepsilon ; all steps before it are forecast. Three safeguards apply. The first 3 3 steps of sampling are always computed, giving the filters real observations to establish values and trends; the final step is always computed, so the sample is finished by a true model evaluation; and the number of consecutive skips is capped at 10 10 regardless of the predicted risk. The threshold ε \varepsilon is set once for each compute budget. Starting from a range of candidate values, we run the scheduler on a set of calibration prompts that are not used for evaluation and measure the average number of transformer calls. If the average is above the target, we raise ε \varepsilon ; if it is below, we lower it. We repeat this, halving the range each time, until the average matches the target. At inference, ε \varepsilon is kept fixed, but the number of transformer calls is not. The risk depends on the per-band scale κ ~ ℓ \tilde{\kappa}_{\ell} , which is updated from the errors observed during each generation. A generation whose trajectory is easy to forecast accumulates risk slowly and uses fewer calls than the target, while a harder one uses more. The target is therefore met on average rather than for every generation, and the number of calls varies around the target from one generation to the next.

sections.heading: D.3 Fixed-Schedule Variant
sections.text: As a deterministic alternative, we support a fixed schedule with linearly growing gaps, computing steps j r = ⌊ α r ( r + 1 ) / 2 ⌋ , r = 1 , 2 , … , j r < N − 1 , j_{r}=\big\lfloor\alpha\,r(r{+}1)/2\big\rfloor,\qquad r=1,2,\dots,\quad j_{r}<N-1, (50) together with the warm-up steps { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} and the final step, where α \alpha is chosen by a simple search so that the total number of computed steps matches the target budget. The spacing is dense early in sampling, where the output changes fastest, and sparse late, similar to the schedules the adaptive scheduler produces for typical generations. The fixed variant is preferable when a deterministic compute cost is required, while the adaptive variant reallocates calls between easy and hard generations at the same average cost. In Table 3 , the adaptive variant improves PSNR by 2.2 dB over the fixed variant at the same budget.

sections.heading: Appendix E Models with Classifier-Free Guidance
sections.text: Some of the evaluated models use classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) at inference. For these models, each denoising step runs the transformer twice, once with the prompt and once with the negative prompt, and combines the conditional output Y j c Y^{c}_{j} and the unconditional output Y j u Y^{u}_{j} into a guided velocity Y j = 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y j c , Y j u ) , 𝒢 ⁡ ( c , u ) = u + w ⁡ ( c − u ) , Y_{j}=\mathcal{G}\big(Y^{c}_{j},Y^{u}_{j}\big),\qquad\mathcal{G}(c,u)=u+w\,(c-u), (51) where w w is the guidance scale. Some models modify 𝒢 \mathcal{G} ; Qwen-Image, for example, rescales each token of the guided velocity to the norm of the conditional prediction ( Eq. 55 ).

sections.heading: Forecasting the guided velocity.
sections.text: SpecKCast forecasts the transformer output rather than its internal features, so it can be placed outside the network. For models with CFG, we place it after the guidance combination and forecast the guided velocity Y j Y_{j} , which is the quantity the sampler uses, with a single forecaster. On a computed step, both passes run, Y j Y_{j} is formed with the model’s own 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , and the forecaster is updated with it. On a skipped step, neither pass runs and the forecast Y ^ j \widehat{Y}_{j} is passed to the sampler. The frequency bands, time coordinates, Kalman filters, and scheduler are the same as for models without guidance, which correspond to 𝒢 ⁡ ( c , u ) = c \mathcal{G}(c,u)=c . With n n computed steps out of N N , SpecKCast therefore uses 2 ​ n 2n transformer passes instead of 2 ​ N 2N .

sections.heading: Relation to forecasting each pass separately.
sections.text: An alternative is to forecast Y j c Y^{c}_{j} and Y j u Y^{u}_{j} separately on the same schedule and combine the two forecasts with 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . Suppose the forecast at a skipped step k k is a linear combination of the outputs observed at earlier computed steps, Y ^ k = ∑ j ∈ 𝒰 , j < k a k , j ​ Y j , \widehat{Y}_{k}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U},\,j<k}a_{k,j}\,Y_{j}, (52) where the weights a k , j a_{k,j} do not depend on the observed values. If, in addition, 𝒢 ⁡ ( c , u ) = w ​ c + ( 1 − w ) ​ u \mathcal{G}(c,u)=w\,c+(1-w)\,u with the same w w at every step, then ∑ j a k , j ​ 𝒢 ​ ( Y j c , Y j u ) = w ​ ∑ j a k , j ​ Y j c + ( 1 − w ) ​ ∑ j a k , j ​ Y j u = 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ^ k c , Y ^ k u ) , \sum_{j}a_{k,j}\,\mathcal{G}\big(Y^{c}_{j},Y^{u}_{j}\big)=w\sum_{j}a_{k,j}\,Y^{c}_{j}+(1-w)\sum_{j}a_{k,j}\,Y^{u}_{j}=\mathcal{G}\big(\widehat{Y}^{c}_{k},\widehat{Y}^{u}_{k}\big), (53) so forecasting the guided velocity gives the same output as forecasting each pass and combining the forecasts. Taylor extrapolation and the Chebyshev fit used by Spectrum have the form of Eq. 52 , and so does a Kalman filter with fixed noise parameters, since its gains do not depend on the observed values. In SpecKCast, the equivalence is no longer exact because the process noise is adapted online from the observed errors, which makes the weights a k , j a_{k,j} depend on the observations. It is also not exact when 𝒢 \mathcal{G} includes a nonlinear correction such as the norm rescaling of Qwen-Image. We forecast the guided velocity because it is the quantity the sampler uses, so the forecast error and the scheduling risk are measured directly on what affects the sample, and because it requires a single set of filter states instead of two.

sections.heading: Variants.
sections.text: We also implement two variants, which are not used in the reported experiments. The per-branch variant runs one forecaster for each branch on a shared schedule, set by the conditional branch, and combines the two forecasts with 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . The asymmetric variant gives each branch its own schedule and compute budget, so a step can run neither pass, only one, or both. Writing Eq. 51 as Y j = w ​ Y j c − ( w − 1 ) ​ Y j u Y_{j}=w\,Y^{c}_{j}-(w-1)\,Y^{u}_{j} shows that an error in the unconditional forecast is scaled by w − 1 w-1 , while an error in the conditional forecast is scaled by w w . sections.heading: G.2 PCA Construction and Display
sections.text: Both models use the same procedure for joint views and normalization, applied independently to each model. For each prompt and panel, we arrange the recorded values into a coefficient-by-step matrix and divide it by its Frobenius norm. For a joint view, the 12 normalized matrices are concatenated along the coefficient axis and transposed, giving a matrix with 50 observations and 12 ​ d 12d features, where d d is the number of retained entries in that panel. We center each feature across steps and project onto its first two principal components. Thus, each joint curve summarizes temporal variation across all 12 generations. For the individual views, the same procedure is applied to each prompt separately, giving a distinct PCA basis for each prompt and panel. Within each panel, both score sequences are divided by their joint maximum absolute value. This shared scaling preserves the relative geometry of the two displayed components. For both models, the PCA is computed by singular value decomposition, PC1 is oriented so that its final score is at least its initial score, and PC2 is oriented so that its score at step 25 is nonnegative. Within each joint figure, all rows use exactly the same normalized scores, as do the paired three-dimensional and planar views for each individual prompt. Planar views use equal axis scaling and shared square limits. Circles mark measured states, blue changes from dark to light with denoising progress, and stars mark the final state (PC1 in the score-versus-step view). Straight segments connect successive measurements without smoothing.

Brown Affiliation: AI Center–Toronto, Samsung Electronics Abstract Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity image and video generation, but they suffer from substantial inference costs due to repeated transformer evaluations across many denoising steps. Feature caching reduces this cost by reusing features across denoising steps. Recent forecasting methods extend this idea by extrapolating features to skipped steps instead of reusing them. However, existing forecasting methods extrapolate the features they predict uniformly, even though the spatial-frequency components of these features change most at different stages of denoising. They also overlook that denoising progresses nonuniformly, so equal step intervals can correspond to very different amounts of change. These mismatches amplify forecast errors as more steps are skipped, limiting the achievable acceleration. We propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that forecasts the model output in the frequency domain. SpecKCast applies a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the output and tracks each coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter along a band-specific time coordinate derived from the noise schedule. The filter tracks each coefficient’s value and rate of change, and the transformer is evaluated only when the filter’s forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo show that SpecKCast achieves a better trade-off between acceleration and fidelity than existing caching and forecasting methods, reaching up to 6 × 6\times speedup with less than 0.05 GiB of additional memory. Figure 1: Qualitative comparison on FLUX at different acceleration ratios. 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity visual generation, gaining significant attention from recent advances in image and video generation. Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) further improved generation quality by enabling greater model capacity. However, their costly forward passes throughout many denoising steps lead to substantially higher inference latency, limiting their use in real-time applications. To address this bottleneck, a wide range of acceleration techniques have been proposed to reduce either the step count or the per-step cost, including efficient attention ( Xia et al., 2025 ) , step distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , and quantization ( Li et al., 2023 ) . Among these, feature caching has emerged as a practical, training-free approach. Motivated by the observation that model outputs are highly similar across adjacent timesteps, these methods cache features from previous steps and reuse them in subsequent ones, skipping substantial computation ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) . However, this similarity decays as the gap between timesteps grows, so naive reuse over longer spans significantly degrades generation quality, limiting caching to modest acceleration ratios. To address this, recent work shifts from reusing features to forecasting them ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Rather than assuming that a cached feature remains valid at a later timestep, forecasting methods exploit temporal continuity along the denoising trajectory, using features from previous steps to estimate their evolution and extrapolate their values at the target timestep. By modeling temporal drift, forecasting remains effective across wider timestep gaps, enabling higher acceleration ratios at comparable generation quality. Despite their promise, existing forecasting approaches impose uniformity on both what they forecast and how they model the signal over time ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . First, they extrapolate the model output or feature representation as a whole, or apply the same forecasting rule uniformly to all of its components (e.g., channels), even though the spatial-frequency components of the signal evolve very differently. As Figure 2 shows, low-frequency content changes sharply in the first few steps and then settles, while high-frequency content changes slightly at first but evolves rapidly toward the end. Because these bands are active at different stages, a single uniform forecaster may not serve them all. Second, existing methods use the sampler’s step index or raw diffusion timestep as their temporal coordinate, even though the amount of denoising performed at each step is nonuniform and depends on the scheduler. Therefore, equal intervals in the chosen coordinate can represent very different amounts of denoising progress. Treating these intervals as equivalent makes the resulting trajectory harder to model and forecast. Together, these limitations restrict achievable acceleration, amplify forecast errors, and degrade generation quality as the skip length increases. Motivated by this insight, we propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that rethinks both what we forecast and how we extrapolate. The key idea is to forecast the model’s temporal evolution separately in the frequency domain, rather than uniformly in feature or latent space. SpecKCast transforms the model output into the spatial-frequency domain with a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT), and forecasts each coefficient during denoising. Moreover, instead of indexing the trajectory by the sampler’s timestep, SpecKCast exploits a time coordinate derived from the noise scheduler and applies a nonlinear time warping that improves the accuracy of local extrapolation within each band. To track each coefficient as it moves along its trajectory, SpecKCast uses a lightweight Kalman filter, a recursive state-space estimator that maintains the coefficient’s value and rate of change, projecting this state across a skip and correcting it after a full denoising step. The filter also estimates the uncertainty of each forecast. As more steps are skipped, this uncertainty increases, while the rate of change decays to keep the prediction stable. Furthermore, SpecKCast partitions the coefficients into frequency bands that share a common temporal coordinate and forecast uncertainty, while each coefficient keeps its own value and rate of change. Finally, at skipped steps, the predicted coefficients are transformed back to the spatial domain and passed directly to the sampler. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. • Frequency-Decoupled and Scheduler-Aligned Forecasting. We introduce SpecKCast, a training-free method that decomposes the model output in the spatial-frequency domain and forecasts its components along a nonlinear time coordinate derived from the noise scheduler. • Uncertainty-Aware Kalman Forecasting. SpecKCast uses a lightweight Kalman filter to track frequency coefficient trajectories and leverage forecast uncertainty to maintain stability over skipped denoising steps. • State-of-the-Art Performance. SpecKCast consistently improves the acceleration and generation quality trade-off over existing caching and forecasting methods while introducing negligible computational and memory overhead, requiring about 5 MiB of additional memory for FLUX.1 ( Labs, 2024 ) . Additional views, prompts, and Qwen-Image results are in Appendix G . 2 Related work Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) have become a leading approach for image and video generation. Since the introduction of the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , many works have built on this architecture, achieving strong results across diverse domains ( Chen et al., 2024a ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Rajabi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . This progress, however, comes at a cost. Sampling requires many sequential forward passes through a large network, making inference slow and expensive. This limits practical applications and has made diffusion model acceleration an important research direction. A large body of work has therefore focused on reducing sampling steps, mostly by distilling a multi-step teacher into a few-step student ( Meng et al., 2023 ) . Examples include consistency models ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ) and DMD ( Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ) . Although effective, these approaches require additional training and are prone to reduced sample diversity. A more recent line of work explores feature caching, which accelerates inference without any additional training. The core idea is to reuse intermediate features across timesteps to avoid redundant computation ( Zou et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) . Early methods such as DeepCache ( Ma et al., 2024 ) accelerated the U-Net backbone using handcrafted caching rules, and Δ \Delta -DiT ( Chen et al., 2024b ) later extended this idea to DiT architectures. Subsequent methods further refine what and when to cache. FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) reuses attention and MLP outputs across timesteps, while TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) exploits the correlation between timestep embeddings and model outputs to estimate how much the output changes between steps and decide when to reuse cached features. HiCache ( Feng et al., 2026 ) forecasts features with scaled Hermite polynomials to capture their non-monotonic dynamics in DiTs. SeaCache ( Chung et al., 2026 ) instead improves the caching decision by measuring feature changes after a spectral filter that preserves content-relevant components and suppresses noise. However, feature similarity decreases as the timestep gap increases. As more steps are skipped, the cached features deviate further from the actual ones, and these errors accumulate during sampling. This causes the trajectory to drift and degrades generation quality, limiting the achievable speedup. To address this, recent work shifts from reusing features to forecasting them ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Instead of assuming that cached features remain valid at later timesteps, forecasting methods use features from previous steps to predict how they evolve and estimate their values at the target timestep. TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025b ) does this locally with a Taylor expansion, using finite differences of the most recent cached features, while Spectrum ( Han et al., 2026 ) fits a Chebyshev expansion over the full feature history to better capture long-range dynamics. By modeling how features evolve, these methods remain effective over wider timestep gaps, enabling higher acceleration at comparable quality. However, both forecast uniformly in feature space and along the sampler’s timestep, ignoring that denoising progress is nonuniform across steps. In contrast, SpecKCast forecasts each frequency band separately along a scheduler-derived time axis, using a lightweight Kalman filter that adapts its forecasts as the trajectory evolves. 3 Background 3.1 Diffusion Models and Flow Matching Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) define a generative process that gradually transforms samples from a simple prior (e.g., Gaussian) into data via a learned reverse-time process. Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) instead learns a velocity field that transports noise to data along near-straight paths. Both are instances of stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) , with x t = α t ​ x 0 + σ t ​ ϵ x_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon , where rectified flow sets α t = 1 − t \alpha_{t}=1-t and σ t = t \sigma_{t}=t and learns the velocity v = ϵ − x 0 v=\epsilon-x_{0} . Sampling integrates the reverse flow over decreasing noise levels using Euler updates: x j + 1 = x j + ( σ j + 1 − σ j ) ​ Y j , Y j = v θ ​ ( x j , σ j , c ) , x_{j+1}=x_{j}+(\sigma_{j+1}-\sigma_{j})Y_{j},\qquad Y_{j}=v_{\theta}(x_{j},\sigma_{j},c), (1) where c c denotes the text condition. We measure denoising cost by the number of function evaluations (NFE), defined as the number of denoising steps at which the transformer is evaluated; for models with classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , each such step includes both passes. 3.2 Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration Adjacent denoising steps produce highly correlated features and outputs, allowing redundant computation to be avoided ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2026 ) . Forecasting exploits this temporal redundancy by predicting skipped signals from past observations. Let 𝒰 ⊆ { 0 , … , N − 1 } \mathcal{U}\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N-1\} denote the steps that evaluate the denoiser. For output-level forecasting, Y ^ j = f ⁡ ( h j , j ) , j ∉ 𝒰 , \widehat{Y}_{j}=f(h_{j},j),\qquad j\notin\mathcal{U}, (2) where h j h_{j} encodes past outputs and Y ^ j \widehat{Y}_{j} replaces Y j Y_{j} in the sampler. Forecasting may instead target intermediate features, making the choice of forecast target and representation a key design decision. 3.3 Kalman Filter The Kalman filter ( Kalman, 1960 ) is a classical method that recursively estimates the state of a dynamic signal from intermittent observations. It models the state transition as h j = A j ​ h j − 1 + w j , w j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Q j ) , h_{j}=A_{j}h_{j-1}+w_{j},\qquad w_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Q_{j}), (3) y j = H j ​ h j + η j , η j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , R j ) , y_{j}=H_{j}h_{j}+\eta_{j},\qquad\eta_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R_{j}), (4) where A j A_{j} is the state-transition matrix, H j H_{j} maps the state to the observation, and Q j Q_{j} and R j R_{j} are the process- and observation-noise covariances, respectively. The filter alternates between prediction and update , with updates only when observations are available. (5) When an observation y j y_{j} is available, the prediction is corrected using K j = P ¯ j ​ H j ⊤ ​ ( H j ​ P ¯ j ​ H j ⊤ + R j ) − 1 , K_{j}=\overline{P}_{j}H_{j}^{\top}\left(H_{j}\overline{P}_{j}H_{j}^{\top}+R_{j}\right)^{-1}, (6) h ^ j = h ¯ j + K j ​ ( y j − H j ​ h ¯ j ) , P j = ( I − K j ​ H j ) ​ P ¯ j . \widehat{h}_{j}=\overline{h}_{j}+K_{j}(y_{j}-H_{j}\overline{h}_{j}),\qquad P_{j}=(I-K_{j}H_{j})\overline{P}_{j}. (7) Here, K j K_{j} controls the balance between the new observation and the model prediction. An important property of the Kalman filter is that it is fully online, requiring a constant number of operations and no window of past observations to store or refit, so a large number of signals can be tracked in parallel at negligible cost. Between observations, the filter advances the state, while the covariance grows to reflect increasing forecast uncertainty, making the filter suitable for forecasting over extended gaps between observations. 4 Method Spec tral K alman Fore Cast ing (SpecKCast) is an inference-time acceleration method for DiTs that reduces transformer evaluations during denoising. Unlike feature-caching methods that approximate an intermediate activation and still execute the remaining network layers, SpecKCast models the final velocity consumed by the sampler. SpecKCast applies a 2D DCT to the model output and forecasts each frequency coefficient individually, while partitioning coefficients into bands that share forecast uncertainty and a noise-schedule-derived time coordinate, warped nonlinearly to better align with each band’s temporal evolution. SpecKCast uses a Kalman filter to track each DCT coefficient’s value and temporal derivative, while sharing covariance statistics within each frequency band. The predicted coefficients are transformed back to the spatial domain and passed directly to the sampler. 4.1 Frequency-Aware Forecasting 4.1.1 Spatial-frequency Decomposition Forecasting the entire transformer output with a single temporal model ignores an important property of diffusion predictions: different spatial frequencies exhibit different temporal dynamics, as shown in Figure 2 . Low-frequency content settles early and drifts slowly, while high-frequency content remains active until the end of sampling. To account for these distinct dynamics, SpecKCast transforms each output into the spatial-frequency domain and forecasts its coefficients separately. Given the denoiser output Y j ∈ ℝ C × H × W Y_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} at timestep j j , we apply an orthonormal 2D DCT independently to each channel, Z j = DCT 2 ​ D ⁡ ( Y j ) Z_{j}=\operatorname{DCT}_{2\mathrm{D}}(Y_{j}) , and partition the frequency plane into L L non-overlapping radial bands. Each frequency coefficient is treated as a separate temporal signal and forecast by its own predictor, while the band determines how each coefficient’s dynamics are modeled. On steps where the transformer computes the full denoising step, the observed Z j Z_{j} updates the predictors; on skipped steps, the forecasters extrapolate each coefficient’s trajectory and together form Z ^ j \widehat{Z}_{j} . The forecast is then transformed back to the spatial domain, Y ^ j = IDCT 2 ​ D ⁡ ( Z ^ j ) \widehat{Y}_{j}=\operatorname{IDCT}_{2\mathrm{D}}(\widehat{Z}_{j}) , and passed directly to the diffusion sampler. 4.1.2 Band-specific Denoising Time Each coefficient in SpecKCast is forecast as a function of time, which raises the question of what to use as the time variable. A natural choice is the step index j j , but it does not capture the nonuniform progression of the denoising process. As a result, equal increments of j j can correspond to very different amounts of change, making the trajectory harder to forecast. Evaluation. For text-to-image generation, we use the DrawBench ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) prompts and report ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) and CLIP Score ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) , which measures text–image alignment. For text-to-video generation, we follow the standard prompts and protocol of VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and report its Quality Score, which aggregates dimensions such as temporal consistency, motion smoothness, and per-frame aesthetic and imaging quality. Since an accelerated sampler should reproduce the output of the full model rather than merely produce a plausible sample, we also compare each accelerated sample with its 50-step reference generated from the same prompt and seed. We report PSNR for pixel-level error, SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) for structural similarity, and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for perceptual distance. For efficiency, we report sampling latency, speedup over the 50-step reference, and memory overhead (Mem. Δ \Delta ), defined as the peak allocated GPU memory above that of Base at the same NFE. SpecKCast achieves the highest speedup among acceleration methods in all but one setting, along with the best PSNR and LPIPS in all settings and the best SSIM in all but one. At the highest acceleration, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 1.1 dB PSNR on FLUX.1-dev ( 5.54 × 5.54\times ) and 2.0 dB on Qwen-Image ( 6.00 × 6.00\times ). Spectrum, the closest competitor at 14 and 10 NFE, trails SpecKCast by 0.5–1.4 dB PSNR and degrades sharply on Qwen-Image at 8 NFE, where its LPIPS rises to 0.527 compared with 0.267 for SpecKCast. Compared with Base, which runs at a similar speed, SpecKCast improves PSNR by 5.5–9.0 dB, showing that it tracks the 50-step trajectory far more closely than simply taking fewer steps. These gains cost at most 0.01 GiB of memory, whereas TaylorSeer, HiCache, and Spectrum add 0.73–18.97 GiB. Figures 3 and 6 show qualitative results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image, respectively. TaylorSeer and HiCache blur the images, TeaCache and SeaCache alter textures and lighting, and every baseline misspells or distorts the text on the sign. SpecKCast stays closest to the 50-step reference while running fastest. More samples are provided in Appendix F . 5.2 Text-to-video Generation Table 2 reports results on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo. SpecKCast achieves the highest or near-highest speedup in every setting, along with the best SSIM in all settings and the best PSNR and LPIPS in most. On HunyuanVideo at the 14-NFE budget, it improves PSNR by 2.1 dB over SeaCache, the strongest baseline, while running at 3.33 × 3.33\times instead of 2.57 × 2.57\times . The advantage holds at the 8-NFE budget, where SpecKCast keeps the best SSIM and LPIPS on both models, while HiCache and TaylorSeer drop to 12.06 and 13.02 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-14B. SpecKCast also achieves the best VBench Quality on Wan2.1-14B at every budget, staying within 0.25 points of the reference at the 14-NFE budget. Spectrum obtains slightly lower LPIPS on Wan2.1-14B at the 14- and 10-NFE budgets, but requires up to 13.12 GiB of extra memory, compared with 0.05 GiB for SpecKCast. On HunyuanVideo, most baselines replace the puffin in the first frame with a blurred or different bird, and SeaCache adds a second cat in later frames. On Wan2.1-14B, the baselines introduce local artifacts (red boxes), mostly in the window background, and HiCache also shifts the lighting. Since uncertainty-aware scheduling relies on the Kalman covariance, we first compare forecasters under a fixed schedule. Kalman and Taylor perform similarly, with Kalman slightly faster and higher in PSNR, while Chebyshev is both slower and less accurate. With our frequency decomposition and time warping, the Taylor forecaster also outperforms TaylorSeer ( Table 1 ) by 4.2 dB PSNR while reducing latency from 4.59 to 3.46 s. Replacing the fixed schedule with uncertainty-aware scheduling ( Section 4.3 ) improves PSNR by 2.2 dB. Band-specific time warping ( Section 4.1.2 ) outperforms the raw log-SNR λ j \lambda_{j} by 3.3 dB and the step index j j by 4.7 dB, and removing the frequency decomposition lowers PSNR by 3.1 dB. Overall, the full model achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and ImageReward. Since all variants except Chebyshev run within 0.1 s of each other, these gains come at almost no extra latency. 6 Conclusion We presented SpecKCast, a training-free method for accelerating Diffusion Transformers by forecasting the denoiser output at skipped sampling steps. Rather than modeling the output uniformly, SpecKCast decomposes it into spatial-frequency components and forecasts their distinct temporal dynamics along band-specific, noise-schedule-aligned time coordinates. A lightweight Kalman filter tracks the value and rate of change of each DCT coefficient, while its uncertainty provides a principled signal for adaptively determining when a full transformer evaluation is needed. Across image and video diffusion models, SpecKCast consistently improves the acceleration–quality trade-off over existing caching and forecasting methods, achieving the best fidelity to the 50-step reference in most settings with negligible latency and memory overhead. These results highlight the benefit of explicitly accounting for the distinct temporal evolution of frequency components when forecasting diffusion trajectories. SpecKCast, however, targets only temporal redundancy across denoising steps; each computed step still processes the full token grid and therefore retains the spatial redundancy within a transformer evaluation. Jointly exploiting temporal and spatial redundancy could enable further acceleration and represents a promising direction for future work. References Albergo et al. (2025) M. Albergo, N. M.
